Transform group sequential p-values into repeated p-values

Source: R/transform_pvalues_gsd.R
transform_pvalues_gsd.Rd

transform_pvalues_gsd() converts an array of nominal (raw) p-values from a group sequential design into repeated p-values: for each hypothesis and each analysis, the smallest level at which that p-value would cross its alpha-spending boundary. Because the boundary is monotone in the allocated level, the group sequential rejection rule "\(p_{i,k}\) below the boundary for level \(w_i \alpha\)" becomes the fixed-sample rule "\(p^r_{i,k} \le w_i \alpha\)", so a graphical procedure can be run on the transformed values without ever evaluating a boundary.

Usage

transform_pvalues_gsd(
  pvals,
  ...,
  info_frac = NULL,
  spending,
  alpha = 0.025,
  look_back = FALSE,
  grid_size = 1024L
)

Arguments

pvals

A numeric array of raw p-values with dimensions c(nsim, m, K): simulations by hypotheses by analyses.

...

These dots are for future extensions and must be empty.

info_frac

Information fractions. Either a numeric vector of length K, applied to every hypothesis, or an m by K numeric matrix with NA at analyses where a hypothesis has no data. Defaults to the info_frac attribute of pvals.

spending

An alpha-spending function, or a list of m of them (one per hypothesis). A spending function takes a level and a vector of information fractions and returns the cumulative level spent, either as a plain numeric vector or as an object with a spend element (as the gsDesign spending functions do). It must spend the whole level by full information. Any entry may instead be sf_hsd_opt(), which tags a hypothesis whose Hwang-Shih-DeCani parameter is to be optimised by graph_optimise_gsd(); a single sf_hsd_opt() passed on its own is recycled and is one parameter shared by every hypothesis. With any tagged entry the transform returns a spending spec instead (see Value).

alpha

A number giving the overall one-sided significance level. Default is 0.025.

look_back

A logical of length 1 or m. TRUE switches a hypothesis to sequential p-values (see Details). Default is FALSE.

grid_size

A whole number giving the number of allocated levels in each boundary table. Default is 1024.

Value

A multigrain_pvals_gsd object made up of:

  • pvals: the transformed array, of the same dimensions as the input.

  • nsim, m, K: simulations, hypotheses and analyses.

  • alpha: the level the boundary tables were built up to.

  • info_frac: the m by K matrix of information fractions.

  • look_back: the per-hypothesis semantics actually used.

  • spending: a label per spending function.

  • tables: per hypothesis, the analyses that carry distinct information, the analysis at which it matured, and the grid of allocated levels with the nominal boundaries computed at each of them.

When any entry of spending is sf_hsd_opt(), a multigrain_pvals_gsd_spec object instead. It holds the raw p-values (as raw, not pvals), the hypotheses with fixed spending already transformed, the lattice of each spending parameter and one boundary table per lattice node, each checked for well ordering when the spec is built. It is not a multigrain_pvals_gsd object and cannot be passed to calc_power_pvals_gsd(): pass it to graph_optimise_gsd() to optimise the parameters with the graph, or to resolve_pvalues_gsd() to obtain the transformed p-values at chosen values. If every tagged hypothesis has a single analysis at full information, where spending has no effect, an ordinary multigrain_pvals_gsd object is returned with a message.

Details

Boundaries are computed with gsDesign::gsBound1() on a log-spaced grid of allocated levels running from 1e-14 up to alpha, and the resulting monotone table is inverted by log-log linear interpolation.

Per hypothesis, writing \(D\) for the analyses with a non-missing information fraction and \(k^{mat}\) for the first of those that reaches full information (or the last analysis in \(D\) if none does):

  • an analysis without data (NA information fraction) before \(k^{mat}\) is given a repeated p-value of 1, i.e. "cannot reject";

  • analyses after \(k^{mat}\) copy the repeated p-value of \(k^{mat}\) forward, because the statistic of a matured endpoint does not change (it may still be rejected later if recycling gives it more alpha). A non-missing raw p-value supplied after maturity is ignored, with a warning if it differs from the maturity value;

  • a hypothesis with a single analysis at full information is returned unchanged, since there the boundary is the level;

  • if look_back is TRUE for a hypothesis its repeated p-values are replaced by their running minimum over analyses (the sequential p-value), which allows a rejection on the strength of the evidence at any earlier analysis.

If a boundary table is not non-decreasing in the allocated level the spending function is not "well ordered", the group sequential graphical procedure is not valid for it, and the transform aborts.

Examples

# two hypotheses analysed at 60% and 100% of the planned information
set.seed(1)
raw <- array(stats::runif(100 * 2 * 2), dim = c(100L, 2L, 2L))

pvals_gsd <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw,
    info_frac = c(0.6, 1),
    spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF,
    grid_size = 128L
)

pvals_gsd
#> <multigrain_pvals_gsd>
#> 100 simulation(s), 2 hypothes(es), 2 analys(es); alpha = 0.025
#> Information fractions (NA = no data at that analysis):
#>    analysis 1 analysis 2
#> H1        0.6          1
#> H2        0.6          1
#> Look-back: H1 = FALSE, H2 = FALSE
